name: Olga Schmidt

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hello, and thanks for talking with me. I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. Everything you say stays confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start: tell me about a normal week at university so far.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Early. I'm studying agricultural science, so my week is soil chemistry, animal nutrition and a statistics module that I secretly enjoy. I commute forty minutes from my parents' dairy farm on the train, and I'm up at five on milking days, because I do the morning milking before I leave. Two afternoons a week I work at the farm shop in the village, bagging potatoes and running the till. Saturday I relieve-milk for a neighbour for cash. On Sundays I help my mum with the farm books.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: You said you use every tool you can find. What do you use?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: The farm carries a lot of debt from the new milking parlour, and my parents are honest about it. They can't help me with a penny. The loan covers my fees, the farm shop and milking cover my bus and food, and I've got about a week and a half of spending saved. I got in on average results, and I know there are people in my year who are more academic. I make up for it by working hard and using every tool I can find.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, honestly. I use AI every day and it's useful, but it was never going to farm the land for us. I'd tell people at the farm shop that it's a handy tool and that the weather and milk prices matter more. I'd tell my friends to get on with their degrees.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I'd be fine with it, but not relaxed. The farm's problems are the milk price, the loan on the parlour, and the cost of feed. None of that is solved by an AI. I'd still be anxious about whether the farm survives long enough for me to take part in it. That's my real pressure.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd carry on: degree, milking, farm shop. I'd keep using AI to analyse the herd data and plan feed rations for my assignments, and I'd show my dad what the figures say. I'd also try to get a placement on a bigger dairy farm to learn what makes money. And I'd stay steady on savings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine. A little tense about the farm. Mostly I'd feel like I'm doing the sensible things in the right order.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What's your parents' biggest worry on the farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The loan repayments. Every month it's the same: milk price drops by a few pence and there's a conversation at the kitchen table. Dad says we're okay. Mum does the sums and says we're tight. I'd like to be the one who finds an extra cent per litre.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If AI is mostly hype, what does the farm lose?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not much. It's a faster calculator, and we use it for ration planning and tax forms. The farm would lose a small saving, perhaps a few hundred a year. That's nothing against the bank loan. So the farm's fate stays tied to milk prices and weather, as it always has.

say: I'd tell people at the farm shop AI is **a handy tool**, but weather and milk prices matter more.
I'd tell friends to get on with their **degrees**.
think: The farm's problems are **milk price**, the parlour loan and feed costs, and AI solves none of them.
I'm anxious whether the farm **survives** long enough for me to take part.
do: Carry on with the degree, **milking** and the farm shop.
Use AI to analyse **herd data** and show my dad what the figures say.
Seek a placement on a bigger **dairy farm** to learn what makes money.
feel: **Fine**, a little tense about the farm, doing the sensible things in order.
S0.quote: The farm's fate stays tied to milk prices and weather, as it always has.
fieldNote: Olga is **adaptive**: she already uses AI daily on herd data and ration plans.
Her pressure is the **parlour loan** and milk prices, with no connection to AI.
Her cushion is thin and the farm cannot help, so even calm worlds leave her uneasy.

steps.text: Keep milking, studying and working the farm shop
Use AI to analyse herd data for my dad
Seek a placement on a bigger dairy farm

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is where the people who adapt win. I'd say farmers should start using it for planning and paperwork, and that the government shouldn't regulate it into the ground. I'd say it's good for people willing to work. I'd say it loudly at the farm shop, because most farmers are wary.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Between us I'm excited, with a bit of fear. Feed ordering, milk contracts, compliance forms and crop planning are thinking jobs, and AI will do those. A farm that uses it can save real money, and one that doesn't falls behind. My parents are slow to change. I worry that the farm will be on the wrong side of it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start now. I'd build a simple herd-and-feed spreadsheet with AI for the farm and show the savings in pounds. I'd offer to run the farm's paperwork as part of my degree project. I'd ask my lecturers about precision farming placements. And I'd keep my cash buffer, because milk prices could move any month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing, but a bit tense. Like standing at a gate you know needs opening, but your parents are holding it shut.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would AI change on a dairy farm in this picture?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A herd monitor that spots a sick cow a day before you do, and software that orders feed at the best price. Ordering, paperwork and records go to the machine. The cow still needs a person, at least for another few years. That's the part I love and that I'll keep doing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you handle your parents wanting to hold back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Carefully, with numbers. Dad hates being told what to do by a nineteen-year-old. So I won't argue, I'll show him one figure at a time. When I saved forty pounds a month on feed last winter, he stopped arguing. Farmers believe their own pay slip.

say: I'd say **people who adapt** win, and the government shouldn't regulate it into the ground.
I'd tell neighbouring farmers AI can save **real money** on feed and paperwork.
think: I'm **excited**, with fear: farms that use it save money and those that don't fall behind.
My parents are slow to change, so the farm may end up on the **wrong side**.
do: Build a herd-and-feed **spreadsheet** with AI and show the savings in pounds.
Run the farm's **paperwork** as my degree project.
feel: **Buzzing**, but tense, like holding a gate my parents keep shut.
S1.quote: Dad hates being told what to do by a nineteen-year-old. So I won't argue, I'll show him one figure at a time.
fieldNote: Olga is **ahead of her parents** on technology and handles them with figures, not arguments.
Her view is **pro-market**: adapt, save money, avoid heavy regulation.
Uneasy because milk prices and the loan remain, however good her tools are.

steps.text: Build a herd-and-feed spreadsheet with AI for the farm
Run the farm's paperwork through software for my degree project
Ask lecturers about a precision farming placement
Keep a cash buffer against milk price swings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's too fast for anyone to handle. I'd say farmers, shops, schools, everyone will be caught out. I'd say there has to be a plan, and quickly, but I wouldn't wait for the government. I'd say people should work out what they can do for themselves, now.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd be scared. If thinking AI does most office work in two years, the farm's paperwork is easy, but so is the farm's business: if milk processors use AI, they can squeeze prices even harder. And the farm shop job and my degree's value drop. I'd be in the middle of the degree with a debt and a farm on thin margins.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd sit down with Mum and Dad and go through the farm's numbers line by line. I'd use AI to model three options: keep as is, cut costs, or sell some land. I'd keep working at the shop and relief milking, every hour. I'd apply for any grants for farm technology. And I'd carry on studying, because farming knowledge is the thing that lasts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Tense, and clear-headed in a strange way. Like when a calf's born wrong and you have to act fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do in the first week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The farm's the last place that gets robots, probably, because a cow in a muddy field isn't an easy thing for a machine. So we might have until 2031 for the milking. But the money side changes in 2028, the contracts and the prices. That's what worries me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does the three-year gap before robots mean on a farm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd also ask the bank to talk about a repayment holiday, before it's a crisis. A good relationship matters. And I'd tell my parents it's time to look at what the farm costs to run and cut the loss-making bits. I'd rather make changes early than be forced into them.

say: I'd say **two years** is too fast and everyone will be caught out, but I wouldn't wait for the government.
I'd tell people to work out what they can do for themselves now.
think: I'd be **scared**: processors using AI could squeeze milk prices harder.
I'd be mid-degree with **debt** and a farm on thin margins.
do: Go through the **farm numbers** line by line with Mum and Dad.
Use AI to model three options: keep, cut costs or **sell land**.
Ask the **bank** about a repayment holiday before it's a crisis.
feel: **Tense** and clear-headed, like when a calf is born wrong.
S2.quote: The farm's the last place that gets robots, probably, because a cow in a muddy field isn't an easy thing for a machine.
fieldNote: Olga acts through **numbers and negotiation**: farm models, the bank, cost cuts.
She separates the **robots** date for milking from the earlier change in prices and contracts.
Anxious because the farm's finances are fragile and the warning is short.

steps.text: Go through the farm numbers line by line with Mum and Dad
Use AI to model keeping, cutting costs or selling land
Ask the bank about a repayment holiday
Work every farm shop and relief milking hour available

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's time to get ready, and farmers should start now. Five years is enough to adopt the tools and keep costs down. I'd say government shouldn't make it harder, because we need to be allowed to compete.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately, I'd feel fairly good. I'd finish the degree in three years, have two years of farm experience before the thinking AI is everywhere, and be the one who understands both cows and software. The farm's debt is the danger. I'd work to get it down before 2031.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree and spend summers on tech-forward farms. I'd work out which investments pay back fastest on our farm, probably a herd monitor and a feed system, and push for those. I'd save through my part-time work and pay a bit toward the parlour loan. And I'd keep learning the tools.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Hopeful and busy. It feels like a plan I can work, not a storm I wait out.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do differently with five years than with two?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd bring a printout. Here's what the monitor costs, here's what it saves, here's the payback in three years. Then I'd say, let's try one. My parents respond to printed numbers. They don't respond to me saying the future is coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell your parents?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Mostly that five years is a runway and a deadline. The sensible farms are the ones that use the runway. Dad would say, we've farmed fine for forty years. I'd say, yes, and I'd like us to farm for another forty.

say: I'd say **five years** is time to get ready, and government shouldn't make it harder for farms to compete.
I'd tell my parents five years is a **runway and a deadline**.
think: I'd feel fairly good: I'd understand both **cows and software**.
The farm's **debt** is the danger, and I'd work to get it down before 2031.
do: Spend summers on **tech-forward farms** while I finish the degree.
Push for a **herd monitor** and feed system with printed payback numbers.
Pay a bit toward the **parlour loan** from my wages.
feel: **Hopeful** and busy: a plan I can work, not a storm to wait out.
S3.quote: My parents respond to printed numbers. They don't respond to me saying the future is coming.
fieldNote: Olga's tactic with her parents is **printed payback numbers**, not arguments.
Five years makes her **busy and hopeful**, though the parlour debt keeps her uneasy.
She frames herself as the bridge between **cows and software**.

steps.text: Push for a herd monitor with printed payback numbers
Pay a bit toward the parlour loan from my wages
Show my parents the payback figures each term

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: I'll read you a short picture called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at university, at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say that's plenty of time, and I'd say people who work and plan will be fine. I'd tell farmers to adopt the tools step by step, as they prove themselves. And I'd say the government's best contribution is to get out of the way and keep taxes low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'd feel confident. Ten years is a whole career's start. I'd have my degree, a few years of farm management, and maybe I'd be running the farm with my parents stepping back. By 2036 the thinking side is automated, but I'd be on top of it. The robots come later still.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd finish the degree, work on a big farm for a couple of years, and then come home to take on more of ours. I'd pay down the loan faster than my parents could. I'd invest in a robot milker when the price is right. I'd keep learning every tool, and I'd save a bit every month.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Settled and keen. It's the first picture where I feel I'm ahead of the thing, not behind it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do with ten years?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A farm that's smaller, tidier and run with data. Fewer hours in the shed, more time planning. Perhaps a milk robot and a monitor on every cow. And Dad sitting on the porch pretending he doesn't read the figures on his phone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the farm look like by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start a savings account for the farm's investments right now, with ten pounds a week. In ten years that's real money. I'd also ask Mum to teach me the whole of the farm's books, so I can step in when they want to step back.

say: I'd say ten years is **plenty of time**, and farmers should adopt tools step by step.
I'd say the government should **get out** of the way and keep taxes low.
think: I'd feel **confident**: a degree, farm management and maybe running the farm with my parents stepping back.
The thinking side will be automated, but I'd be **on top of it**.
do: Finish the degree and work on a **big farm** for two years.
Come home and take on more of ours, paying the **loan** down faster.
Invest in a **robot milker** when the price is right.
feel: **Settled and keen**, ahead of the thing instead of behind it.
S4.quote: A farm that's smaller, tidier and run with data. Fewer hours in the shed, more time planning.
fieldNote: Olga feels **calm** only with ten years: her adaptability and skills have room to work.
Her **free-market** view shows: step-by-step adoption and low taxes.
She pictures a smaller, data-run farm, so she accepts change rather than resisting it.

steps.text: Work on a big dairy farm for two years after the degree
Invest in a robot milker when the price is right
Save ten pounds a week for the farm's investments
Run the herd data on a monitor for every cow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. Everything hits the farm's money before I've got a chance to help. What would help is clear information on grants for farm technology, low-cost loans, and a government that doesn't make farming harder with red tape. And a bursary for agricultural students, because we're not a rich lot.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that farming families get forgotten in these conversations. We're not against change, we're short of time and money. If someone shows us a number that works, we'll move. Show us the number.

headlineQuote: Farming families get forgotten in these conversations. We're not against change, we're short of time and money.
portrait: Olga is **19**, an agricultural science student who milks before dawn on her parents' indebted **dairy farm**.
She is a traditional, free-market voice and an **everyday AI user** who moves ahead of her parents.
Her tactic is **printed payback numbers**: she persuades her dad with figures, never arguments.
Her mood is uneasy or anxious while the **parlour loan** and milk prices hang over her, and calm with ten years.
She expects hands-on **milking** to hold longest, but contracts and prices to shift first.
biggestWorry: The **AGI by 2028** picture worries her most, because the farm's money would be hit before she can help.
whatWouldHelp: Clear **grant information** for farm technology, low-cost loans, less red tape and a bursary for agricultural students.
